seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

msIdentifier.repository: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library, Yale University

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p: Dear Pound: Thanks for card of 21 ult. It was 17 days on the way. I understand that all letters must now bear, besides the signature, the full name and address of sender. No news about my novel and, of course, not a word from my agent . I hope Mr Knoblock likes my play. The following may interest you. A Mr Gray who is interned with my brother read my stories but said he disliked A Painful Case . He knew the woman, a Mrs –, and the husband was second officer on the Holyhead-Kingstown Line and he remembered the night she was run over at Sydney Parade station and the finding of a bottle in her jacket. My brother asked when this happened. He answered in the autumn of 1909. My brother (who tells this curious history in a letter to my wife) replied: “My brother wrote the story in Pola, Austria, in 1905”. I had a reply from Mr Marsh , very polite and kind. Χαίρετε , as Ulysses would say.

div.note: British wartime postal censorship intensified in 1916 (John Ferris, “Postal Censorship and the Alchemy of Victory at Sea during the First World War,” in Economic Warfare and the Sea: Grand Strategies for Maritime Powers, 1600-1945, ed. David Morgan-Owen and Louis Halewood [Liverpool, UK: Liverpool University Press, 2020], 187-90.)

JJ’s London agent J.B. Pinker wrote him on 16 October 1916 that he was negotiating the contract for the American edition of A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man with the New York publisher B.W. Huebsch, who wanted an option on JJ’s next book and sheets for publishing Dubliners. Royalties for A Portrait were to be 10% on the first 2,000 copies sold, then 15%. JJ was to receive £10 advance on royalties upon signing (John Firth, “James Pinker to James Joyce, 1915–1920,” Studies in Bibliography 21 [1968]: 216-17). Huebsch published A Portrait in December 1916.

In September 1916, Pound met with the playwright and novelist Edward Knoblock in London in an effort to interest him in adapting JJ’s play Exiles for the stage. Nothing came of this meeting (see JJ to Pound, 14 September 1916, notes).

JJ’s brother Stanislaus (1884-1955), who had strong views about Austria and Italy, was arrested in January 1915 and interned in Austrian detention centers until the end of the conflict (Ellmann, JJ 380).

In JJ’s Dubliners story, “A Painful Case,” which he rewrote in Trieste in the spring of 1905 (Ellmann, JJ 207), the main character, James Duffy – partly based on Stanislaus – enters into a Platonic relationship with Emily Sinico, a woman married to a mercantile sea captain. Duffy abruptly breaks with Mrs. Sinico when one evening, after listening to him talk about himself and his ideas, she impulsively presses his hand to her cheek. Four years later, Duffy learns that Mrs. Sinico has been struck and killed by the train from Kingstown at Sydney Parade Station in Dublin. It is hinted that she had taken to drink. The story ends with Duffy in the Phoenix Park at night, feeling isolated and alone.

Kingstown was a town and seaport on Dublin Bay, and was renamed Dún Laoghaire in 1920. Mail steamers and express boats carrying passengers regularly plied the Irish Sea between Kingstown and Holyhead in Wales. Sandycove, near Kingstown, was and is the site of the Martello tower where JJ stayed with Oliver St. John Gogarty for a few days in 1904, and which JJ used for the opening scenes of Ulysses.

On 13 September 1916, JJ wrote Edward Marsh, assistant private secretary to British Prime Minister H.H. Asquith, to thank him for helping him obtain a grant of £100 from the British Civil List (LI 94) (For the circumstances of the grant, see JJ to Pound, 14 September 1916, notes.)

Gk. χαίρετε means “hail!” or “farewell!” The verb χαίρω is literally “I rejoice.” JJ uses here the second person plural imperative. He is correct that Ulysses would have said it, since modern and ancient (including Homeric) Greek forms are identical in this case. (Thanks to Stephanie Nelson for assistance with the Greek.)
